nodes.location: Front of the abdomen, at the surface: one strap on each side of the midline, from the pubic bone up to the lower end of the breastbone and the lower ribs.

nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: A surface muscle at the front of the abdomen (kenhub.rectus_abdominis, imaios.rectus_abdominis); Kenhub says it is clearly visible beneath the skin in people with low body fat. nodes.layerCheck: §1.2 'surface': supported (Kenhub: on the anterior surface of the abdominal wall). It lies inside the rectus sheath, whose front wall is the tendon sheets of the side muscles (imaios.rectus_abdominis), and the small pyramidalis lies in front of its lowest part (elsevier.rectus_abdominis); neither is a muscle belly over it, so 'surface' holds. §1.2's 'one node (drawn in segments)' matches the anatomy: the tendinous intersections divide one muscle.

nodes.name: External oblique
nodes.databaseMuscleNote: Seen in the recorded database fixture (server/fixtures/liveMuscleAggregation.ts: 'External oblique', muscle_group 'obliques') and in shared/capabilityRank.ts.
nodes.location: Side and front of the abdomen, at the surface: from the outer faces of the lower eight ribs to the crest of the hip bone, the pubic bone and the midline band.
nodes.whatItDoes: With both sides working, bends your trunk forward and presses on the abdomen. With one side working, bends the trunk to that side and turns it toward the other side.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the contour of the side of the waist and, where its slips interlock with the serratus anterior, of the lower ribs at the side of the chest. Toward the front it becomes a thin tendon sheet, which is not muscle bulk. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Twisting work loads it together with the internal oblique of the other side, which turns the trunk the same way; how the work splits between them is not known.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: The most superficial of the flat muscles (kenhub.external_abdominal_oblique, teachmeanatomy.abdominal_wall, imaios.external_abdominal_oblique), but only its side part is muscle: toward the front it becomes an aponeurosis that covers the rectus abdominis (kenhub.external_abdominal_oblique). 'partial' is an inference from that.
nodes.layerCheck: §1.2 'surface': supported by three references. For the drawing lane: its belly is at the side; the part in front of the rectus abdominis is tendon sheet, drawn as structure or not at all.

nodes.location: Abdominal wall, deepest layer: wraps around the abdomen from the lower ribs, the fascia of the lower back and the hip bone to the midline band at the front.

claims.statement: The rectus abdominis lies at the surface of the front of the abdomen, one strap on each side of the midline band (linea alba), from the pubic bone up to the lower end of the breastbone and the cartilages of the fifth to seventh ribs. It sits inside a sheath formed by the tendon sheets of the other abdominal muscles. Tendinous bands cross it, usually three, at about the level of the lower end of the breastbone, the navel and midway between them, and divide it into segments; in people with low body fat these segments can show beneath the skin. It may therefore contribute to the front contour of the abdomen. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

sources.title: Kenhub: Rectus abdominis: Origin, insertion, innervation, function
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q5, Q42, Q49, Kenhub only). Function: trunk flexion, compression of the abdominal viscera, and expiration (Q5, tied to 'Kenhub's muscle page'). Location: a paired muscle running vertically either side of the linea alba on the front of the abdominal wall, from the pubic crest and symphysis to the xiphoid process and the cartilages of ribs 5-7; three tendinous intersections, at the xiphoid, the umbilicus and midway, sometimes four; 'In those with low body fat, it is clearly visible beneath the skin forming the six pack'. sources.title: Sarti MA, Monfort M, Fuster MA, Villaplana LA. Muscle activity in upper and lower rectus abdominus during abdominal exercises. Arch Phys Med Rehabil 1996;77(12):1293-7
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q30, Q32): PubMed abstract. Nonrandomized trial, convenience sample of 33 healthy volunteers split by activity level and by whether they performed the exercises correctly; surface EMG (average iEMG) of the upper and lower rectus abdominis in curl-ups and posterior pelvic tilts. Correct performers: curl-ups gave greater upper-part activity in both activity groups; the pelvic tilt worked the lower part harder than the curl-up only in the high-activity correct-performer subgroup; incorrect performers activated both parts about equally. Abstract only.

sources.title: Electromyographic comparison of the upper and lower rectus abdominis during abdominal exercises. J Strength Cond Res 2003;17(3):475-83
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q30, Q33): PubMed abstract of a pilot study; eight healthy adults, six abdominal exercises in random order (including the curl-up, a curl-up on an exercise ball and leg lowering); no significant difference between upper and lower rectus abdominis EMG in any exercise. sources.title: Escamilla RF, Babb E, DeWitt R, et al. Electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Phys Ther 2006;86(5):656-71
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q28, Q31, Q46). The abstract was seen through a search summary beside a Sacramento State repository record (scholars.csus.edu): surface EMG of 21 healthy adults aged 23-43, normalised to maximum voluntary contractions, from the upper and lower rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques, rectus femoris, latissimus dorsi and lumbar paraspinals; upper and lower rectus abdominis, internal oblique and latissimus dorsi activity highest in roll-outs, pikes and knee-ups on a wheeled device, hanging knee-ups with straps and reverse crunches on a 30-degree incline; external oblique highest in the wheeled-device exercises and hanging knee-ups with straps; the same exercises most effective at activating extraneous muscles; lumbar paraspinal activity low and similar across exercises. The full list of exercises compared was not shown. The PMID 16649890 and the author list come from secondary citations (two blog posts and a magazine article), not from PubMed; the DOI was given by one of them and by the summary. Not to be confused with the same first author's 2006 JOSPT paper on commercial devices (PubMed 16494072). The wheeled device is named by its brand in the abstract; athlete copy does not name it.

sources.title: Snarr RL, Esco MR. Electromyographical comparison of plank variations performed with and without instability devices. J Strength Cond Res 2014;28(11):3298-3305
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q38, Q39): abstract seen through a summary beside the BISp sports-literature record and university repository listings. Twelve healthy adults (six men, six women), isometric holds of five plank variations in random order; EMG of the rectus abdominis, external oblique and erector spinae; planks on instability devices produced higher activity in these surface muscles than the stable plank; the authors advise caution for people with lower-back weakness because erector spinae activity rose. The devices themselves were not named in the abstract excerpt (a 2017 write-up the summary linked to the study mentions an exercise ball and a suspension device; not used). PMID not seen.

sources.title: Urquhart DM, Hodges PW. Differential activity of regions of transversus abdominis during trunk rotation. Eur Spine J 2005;14(4):393-400
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q35, Q45): abstract on Springer Medicine and the University of Queensland's publication listing. Six people with no history of spinal pain; fine-wire electrodes in the upper, middle and lower transversus abdominis and in the obliques, surface electrodes over the rectus abdominis; seated trunk rotation in both directions. The transversus abdominis was active throughout rotation, its upper fibres recruited in the opposite pattern to its middle and lower fibres; the rectus abdominis showed no directional difference. A later commentary in the same results reads it as activity in both directions, stronger when the chest turns toward the muscle's side, and notes the muscle's small moment arm for rotation. PMID not seen.

sources.title: Tayashiki K, Takai Y, Maeo S, Kanehisa H. Intra-abdominal Pressure and Trunk Muscular Activities during Abdominal Bracing and Hollowing. Int J Sports Med 2016;37(2):134-143
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q26, Q44): abstract on Thieme Connect. Seven young adult men; pressure inside the abdomen measured with a rectal transducer, with surface EMG of the rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique and erector spinae. The rise in pressure was far greater in bracing than in hollowing; at peak pressure activity was higher in bracing than hollowing and higher in the internal oblique than in the other three muscles; pressure and muscle activity were linearly related in both tasks, with a task-specific relationship. The transversus abdominis was not recorded. Abstract only; PMID not seen.

sources.title: The prevalence and consequences of abdominal rectus muscle diastasis among Finnish women: an epidemiological cohort study
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q41, Q48): abstract (PMC, Springer and Springer Medicine copies). Prospective cohort at Helsinki University Hospital; linea alba width measured by ultrasound at the early pregnancy scan in 933 women; mean width about 1.81 cm in women with no earlier pregnancy, about 2.36 cm after one and 2.55 cm after more, rising with the number of earlier pregnancies; severe diastasis (over 5 cm) rare; moderate diastasis not explaining back pain or disability at the population level. Authors not shown; the journal (Hernia) and the year 2021 are inferred from the DOI by the summary.

disagreements: Transversus abdominis and turning the trunk: Kenhub lists ipsilateral rotation on one-sided contraction; Radiopaedia, IMAIOS and Elsevier list compression only (Q10, Q11, Q21). The function claim states the disagreement; no spine.rotation node action is recorded. The fine-wire study (springer.transversus_rotation_emg) shows it active during turning, which is activity, not torque; a commentary in the same results calls its moment arm for rotation small.

External oblique, side of lateral flexion: Kenhub (and anatomy.app, not cited) say the same side; LearnMuscles (not cited) gives no side; Elsevier says 'laterally flexes' with no side. The claim says 'to that side', the anatomical reading of Kenhub's 'ipsilateral'.

Rectus abdominis and side bending: one unidentified physiotherapy source (Q15) and an IMAIOS veterinary entry say it helps bend the trunk sideways; no human anatomy reference cited here lists it. Not claimed; no spine.lateral_flexion node action.
Rectus abdominis and tilting the pelvis back: mentioned by an untied line in Q1 and by LearnMuscles for the group (Q7); not confirmed by Kenhub (Q5). Not claimed (not a region action either).

Upper versus lower rectus abdominis: Sarti 1996 found differences in correct performers; the 2003 pilot found none; a later paper groups Lehman and McGill 2001 with the studies finding none (Q29, abstract not seen, not cited). The selectivity claim says the question is unsettled.

Number of tendinous intersections: three in most references; three to four (IMAIOS, a Kenhub video); one to five in two cadaver series. The appearance claim says 'usually three'; the variation claim gives the range.

Pressure in the abdomen as a spine stabiliser: contested (Q27: a review argues the proposed mechanism lacks experimental support; a thesis says it cannot be determined with certainty). Kenhub's line that the abdominal muscles 'stabilize the vertebral column' with the back muscles is not used. No claim says that bracing steadies the spine.
Rectus abdominis and compression, prime or assist: MeSH (Gray's) says it 'assists'; Kenhub, IMAIOS and Elsevier list compression unqualified. Recorded as assist (see nodeActions).
notes.abdomenCompression: What the evidence supports about abdomen.compression (bracing, raising pressure in the abdomen): every anatomy reference cited lists compressing the abdomen as an action of the three flat muscles; for the transversus abdominis it is the main and, in three of four references, the only action, with raising intra-abdominal pressure named by Radiopaedia, Kenhub and IMAIOS; the internal oblique (five references) and the external oblique (Kenhub, Elsevier) compress the abdomen when both sides act; the rectus abdominis 'assists' (MeSH) or compresses (Kenhub, IMAIOS, Elsevier). One measured study (thieme.bracing_hollowing_iap, seven men, abstract only) found that bracing raised the pressure far more than drawing the belly in, that pressure and muscle activity rose together, and that the internal oblique was the most active of the four trunk muscles recorded; the transversus abdominis was not recorded. Not supported here, so not claimed: that raised pressure steadies the spine (contested, Q27); that the diaphragm and pelvic floor share the work (seen only in a thesis and a blog, Q27); any figure for how much each muscle contributes (the 1992 intramuscular study, Q22 and Q24, was seen only as a reference-list entry). Node actions: transversus abdominis, internal oblique and external oblique prime; rectus abdominis assist.
deliberatelyNotClaimed: Rectus abdominis lateral flexion and pelvic tilt (no cited human anatomy reference).
Expiration: named for the internal oblique and transversus abdominis in their claims, but not a region action, so no node action.

The transversus abdominis's early activation before arm and leg movements, and its timing in people with low back pain: a known clinical literature, not searched as a selectivity claim (it is not about which exercise loads which muscle); results in Q45 also show it is disputed.

Plank and side-plank variations beyond the one tied abstract: the long-lever posterior-tilt plank (Q37), side-bridge variants (Q36, Q50) and suspended planks (Q39) were found only as citations or untied summaries.
Anti-rotation work (a press held against a sideways pull): the only EMG study found (Q39) is a small methodology study in a conference-abstract series; not cited.
The 1998 intramuscular study of psoas and the abdominal wall across many tasks (Q34): abstract not seen.
Any statement that a muscle grows, or how much an exercise loads it: no claim says either.
